claim_verdicts.evidence: The -v run shows SSH2_MSG_KEXINIT sent/received, "kex: algorithm: mlkem768x25519-sha256", SSH2_MSG_KEX_ECDH_REPLY, then SSH2_MSG_NEWKEYS before any authentication: an exchange precedes the ciphered traffic. It cannot show that the shared secret is never itself sent. RFC 4253 governs; it is not a docs root in versions.yaml and not in refs/rfc. Kind behavior; not blocking.

The -v run shows the diagram's order: "Offering public key: /keys/lab_key ED25519 SHA256:/WwGJ...", then "Server accepts key: /keys/lab_key ...", then "Authenticated to localhost ([::1]:2222) using "publickey"." What the signature covers (data of this session) is not visible at debug1, and RFC 4252 s.7 is neither a permitted root nor mirrored in refs/rfc. Kind behavior; not blocking.

claim_verdicts.evidence: No permitted source: versions.yaml has no root for scp, rsync or the history of putting software on machines, and refs/ holds nothing on it. The scp run only shows a file can be copied over SSH, not how common the practice was or is. Kind history; not blocking, but see the minor on sections 5, 8 and 9.

That the user-auth signature covers session-unique data is RFC 4252 s.7 material; not a permitted root, not in refs/rfc. debug1 output does not show the signed data, and a replay test would need capturing and re-injecting packets, which this review could not do. Kind behavior; not blocking.

Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])?"; without a tty: "Host key verification failed." So ssh records the key only once you accept it. claim_verdicts.suggested_text: During key exchange the server signs the exchange with the private half of its host key pair; the first time, ssh normally shows that key's fingerprint and records the public half only once you accept it, and on later connections it refuses a machine whose key differs from the record.

issues.quote: its working directory and every path it opens are that machine's
issues.text: 'working directory' is not in known_vocab and not defined in Core concepts. The prerequisite summary lists `pwd` and `cd` but never names the idea, so I cannot tell whether it means something other than 'the folder the shell is in'.
issues.fix: Replace 'its working directory and every path it opens' with 'the folder it starts in and every path it opens'.

issues.quote: both ends scramble what they send, so anything carrying it in between cannot read it.
issues.text: Neither the prerequisite nor this lesson says that text travelling between two machines passes through anything else. So 'anything carrying it in between' (Core concepts) and 'a machine in between could make the agreement with you itself' (section 4) describe a threat I cannot picture; in this lab both ends are on my own laptop. The whole reason SSH scrambles rests on this.
issues.fix: Add one sentence to the SSH line in Core concepts: on its way between two machines, text usually passes through other machines that forward it, and any of them could read or change it.

issues.quote: The `-o StrictHostKeyChecking` and `-o UserKnownHostsFile` lines switch off the machine check described above
issues.text: The prose explains only what the second option does. Section 4 said `ssh` 'records the public half the first time' but never what `ssh` does on that first time, so I cannot work out what `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` changes, or what I would see if I removed these two lines. 'Host' in both option names is also never tied to 'machine'.
issues.fix: After 'switch off the machine check described above', add one sentence saying what `ssh` normally does when it meets a machine whose key it has not recorded, that `StrictHostKeyChecking=no` skips that step, and that 'host' in the option names means the machine.

issues.quote: Actually the command runs as a process on the far machine, so every path it opens is a path over there.
issues.text: Section 5 just told me 'the box itself reads your laptop's folder whenever something opens a path under /repo', and the only files the lesson's command read were exactly those. So in this lab the misconception looks half true and the correction seems to contradict section 5; I end up unsure whose files `ls -1 /repo/db` read.
issues.fix: Add one sentence to the correction: the path is always looked up on the far machine; `/repo` shows your folder only because the box was set up that way when it started (section 5), not because SSH reached back to your laptop.

issues.quote: From the other machine's disk, where a shell opened for `dev` ran all three commands and sent the output back
issues.text: Section 5 says the box 'reads your laptop's folder whenever something opens a path under /repo: nothing was copied'. So 'from the other machine's disk' reads as wrong to me and 'from your own db folder' feels right. I pick (a) only because (b) and (c) give wrong reasons, not because the lesson supports 'the other machine's disk'.
issues.fix: Reword option a to 'Through the other machine: a shell there, opened for `dev`, opened the path `/repo/db` on that machine and sent the output back', and replace 'reading that machine's disk' in the correct explanation the same way.
